cards.headline: Record revenue can hide a losing business.
cards.body: Revenue is every dollar that came in the door. Profit is what is left after you pay for all of it. A headline about **record revenue** tells you how much money arrived. It says nothing about how much stayed.

art.name: revenue-profit-diverge
art.alt: Revenue rises while profit falls, showing that record sales can hide a losing business.

cards.headline: The top line is only the start.
cards.body: A coffee chain sells **100 million dollars** of coffee in a year. That is revenue — the top line of the income statement. Every cost the business paid to earn it sits below that number, waiting.

art.alt: A coffee shop register records one hundred million dollars of sales before any business costs are paid.

cards.title: Where the money goes

art.alt: A coffee sale moves through four illustrated checkpoints, shrinking from one hundred million dollars of revenue to three million dollars of net income.

cards.caption: Same company, four rungs down. 100 million came in. After beans, staff, rent, interest and tax, **3 million** stayed. That last bar is the business.

cards.headline: First rung: gross profit.
cards.body: Take the 100 million and subtract what the coffee itself cost — beans, milk, cups — 62 million. That leaves **38 million** of gross profit. This is what the product earns before you run a company around it.

art.alt: A coffee receipt subtracts beans, milk, and cups from sales, leaving thirty-eight million dollars of gross profit.

cards.prompt: The chain spends 30 million on staff, rent and marketing. Which line does that come out of?

art.alt: Staff, rent, and marketing bills come out of gross profit and leave eight million dollars of operating income.

cards.explanation: Operating expenses come out of gross profit, not revenue. 38 million minus 30 million leaves **8 million** of operating income — what the business earns from simply operating.

cards.body: Three cuts stand between the top line and the bottom line. Each one asks a different question about the business.

cards.headline: Growing revenue, vanishing profit.
cards.body: Next year the chain opens 40 shops. Revenue climbs to **130 million** — a record. But gross profit only reaches 49 million, new staff and rent cost 47 million, and interest takes 5 million. The year ends at minus 3 million.

art.alt: New coffee shops increase sales while rent, staffing, and interest costs push earnings below zero.

cards.body: Revenue is the top line. What survives every cost, interest and tax is the [[1]] line.
cards.explanation: The bottom line is not a figure of speech. Net income really does sit on the last line of the income statement, under everything the company had to pay.

cards.summary: Revenue measures how much money arrived. Earnings measure how much of it the business managed to keep.
bullets: Revenue minus cost of goods leaves gross profit.
Gross profit minus operating expenses leaves operating income.
Operating income minus interest and tax leaves net income.
Revenue can rise every year while earnings go negative.

art.name: income-waterfall
art.alt: A large revenue column steps down through costs to the smaller earnings the business retains.

cards.insight: Revenue proves people want what you sell. Earnings prove the business can afford to sell it.
